record.paper_title: Nonlinear Schrödinger equation on graphs: recent results and open problems
record.original_question: Can one develop a rigorous mathematical theory for the capture and generation of solitons in nonlinear Schrödinger dynamics on graphs? More specifically, in dynamical regimes that lie between the standing-wave regime and the fast-soliton-scattering regime, can one explain when junction interactions or graph geometry trap a soliton, create a new one, or transfer mass into a localized coherent structure?

evidence.quote: Many interesting physical phenomena experimentally well tested are probably in a different or intermediate region. In particular capture and generation of solitons are not yet understood from a rigorous point of view, and they represent a challenge to mathematical methods and theoretical interpretation where perhaps the simple but non trivial model of NLS equation on graphs could offer some insight.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Let $\mathcal{G}=(V,E)$ be a metric graph: a connected multigraph in which each edge $e\in E$ is identified with an interval $I_e\subset\mathbb{R}$ (finite or half-infinite), and the edges are glued at the vertices. On $\mathcal{G}$ consider the nonlinear Schrödinger (NLS) equation
$$ i\,\partial_t \psi(t,x) = -\Delta_{\mathcal{G}}\,\psi(t,x) - |\psi(t,x)|^{2\sigma}\psi(t,x), \qquad x\in\mathcal{G},\ t\in\mathbb{R}, $$
where $\psi:\mathbb{R}\times\mathcal{G}\to\mathbb{C}$, $\sigma>0$, and $-\Delta_{\mathcal{G}}$ is the Laplacian on $\mathcal{G}$ defined with Kirchhoff (or, more generally, prescribed self-adjoint) boundary conditions at each vertex $v\in V$. A soliton is a solitary-wave solution of the NLS equation on the line $\mathbb{R}$, of the form $\phi_{c,\omega}(x-ct)e^{i\theta(t,x)}$, where $\phi_{c,\omega}$ is the standard NLS soliton profile of speed $c$ and frequency $\omega$.

Two limiting dynamical regimes are well understood:
(i) the standing-wave regime, in which the soliton velocity is small and the solution stays close to a stationary state localized near a vertex;
(ii) the fast-soliton-scattering regime, in which a soliton with large velocity $c\to\infty$ hits a vertex and splits into transmitted/reflected solitons whose amplitudes are governed, to leading order, by the scattering matrix of the linear Laplacian on $\mathcal{G}$.

Problem. Develop a rigorous mathematical theory of soliton dynamics on metric graphs in the intermediate regime between (i) and (ii). Specifically, formulate and prove theorems that, for initial data of the form $\psi_0(x)=\phi_{c,\omega}(x-x_0)$ on an incoming half-line of $\mathcal{G}$ with moderate $c$, characterize quantitatively (in terms of $c$, $\omega$, the vertex conditions, and the topology/geometry of $\mathcal{G}$):
(a) capture: when the soliton is trapped near a vertex or a compact subgraph, converging on long time scales to a localized coherent structure (e.g., a nonlinear bound state);
(b) generation: when a new soliton (not present in the incoming data) emerges on an outgoing edge after the interaction;
(c) mass transfer: the amount of $L^2$-mass that is asymptotically carried by each emerging coherent structure versus radiated away as dispersion.

Provide quantitative criteria (sufficient conditions and, where possible, sharp thresholds) under which (a), (b), or (c) occur.
artifact.status_search_result: No rigorous mathematical theory of soliton capture and generation on metric graphs in the intermediate-velocity regime appears in the literature. Existing rigorous results address either standing waves/ground states or the fast-soliton scattering limit; numerical and physical studies of soliton generation on networks exist but do not provide a rigorous proof. The problem appears to remain open.

status_evidence.title: Soliton generation in optical fiber networks
status_evidence.snippet: Modeling of soliton generation and dynamics in optical fiber networks requires solving NLS on metric graphs; the number of generated solitons is computed numerically for different branching topologies.
status_evidence.claim: Soliton generation on graphs is studied numerically/physically rather than via a rigorous capture-and-generation theorem.
